public_comment.topic: Advocated that participation in after-school sports count as PE/gym credit for high schoolers, citing a student survey and studies on mental health benefits.
Raised concerns about the override not being a permanent fix, wanted long-range financial projections, and described rising need at the local food pantry and community mutual aid.
Reminded residents that the override must pass at both the May 2nd town meeting and the May 16th ballot, and urged attendance at both.
Raised concern that unified sports/arts opportunities for students with disabilities are shrinking and asked for a fuller committee conversation on options.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager approved three capital requests: two feasibility studies for the primary school (playground and drive/playground) and camera systems for building entrances. Other requested items were deferred for later in the year due to funding and the Pacios building situation.

The district is seeking one-time federal earmark funding to build a district-wide instructional framework and offset a projected cut to Title One funding; the district would not have to make up any shortfall if the full amount isn't awarded.
Funds previously voted to be accepted from the scholarship fund were not actually transferred from the estate to students due to a legal/executor issue; the district will bring it back once resolved.
As of month-end the district was at 66.1% of budget expended, rising to 68.6% once a payroll posted; last year the district was at 67% at the same point, having spent less overall.
The collaborative tuition line is overspent because circuit breaker reimbursement money has not yet been posted back into it; this is described as a normally hard line to budget.

Electrical spending is running over budget due to a colder winter and last year's underbudgeting; gas/heating has money remaining, and next year's electrical budget was adjusted based on recent actuals.
Legal expenses are running hot this year and the FY27 budget has been adjusted upward as a result.

The district described fee revenue collected over two periods and the fee schedule by family size and reduced-fee eligibility, and members debated the fairness of the fee against the roughly $70,000 it raises given the district's financial situation.

Chapter 70 does not include transportation costs at all, and regional districts get 75% of transportation reimbursed while Lunenburg does not, which a member said could be worth a large additional sum if reimbursed similarly.

The adult men's basketball program generated minimal revenue per player and relies on unpaid volunteer facilitators; the adult health and fitness program is a pass-through to a private vendor with the district retaining no financial benefit, supporting the recommendation to discontinue the district-run program.

A draft letter to legislators notes Lunenburg ranks near the bottom statewide for per-pupil spending while spending well above the state-required minimum, which members attribute to flaws in how Chapter 70 categorizes districts.
A building-controls efficiency study at the high school may be covered up to 100% by the program, addressing malfunctioning thermostats and actuators causing temperature problems.
The existing landscaping contract for the district's three athletic fields has expired and is going out to bid; costs under the prior contract were described as escalating over the years.
The PTO reported raising a significant amount at a recent dance fundraiser, plus a separate Great Wolf Lodge fundraiser.

Business manager will provide an HR report to the committee, expected to cover the full year.

minutes.headline: Committee voted to keep charging the student bus fee despite members calling it unfair, citing budget desperation.
minutes.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee heard public comment on an override, a student proposal to credit after-school sports as PE, and updates on capital projects and grant-seeking, then worked through a long list of votes: continuing the bus fee, discontinuing the lifelong learning program, approving a $300,000 federal earmark request, and endorsing a letter to legislators on Chapter 70 funding. Facilities updates covered an energy-efficiency program at the high school, relocating a generator from the Pacios building, solar array repairs, and Turkey Hill bathroom renovations, alongside several retirement and new-hire announcements including a new Turkey Hill principal.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to continue charging the student bus fee for another year, despite members calling it unfair, citing the district's financial situation.
Members voted to end the district-run Lunenburg lifelong learning program effective June 1, citing minimal revenue and reliance on volunteers or a pass-through vendor.
The committee authorized the superintendent to pursue a one-time federal earmark to build a district-wide instructional framework and offset an expected cut to Title One funding.
Members endorsed a letter to state legislators arguing Lunenburg's Chapter 70 funding formula undercounts its per-pupil spending and excludes transportation costs.
The FY26 monthly budget report showed spending running ahead of the same point last year, with the electrical and legal lines over budget.

why_it_matters: The bus fee stays in place for families who use it, separate from and regardless of the outcome of the townwide override vote in May.
Ending the lifelong learning program removes a district-run adult offering, though students already enrolled will finish the current session before it closes.
The letter to legislators is an ask, not a change in funding -- any shift in how Chapter 70 treats transportation or per-pupil spending depends on action in Boston, not this committee.
watch_next: Business manager's revolving-fund and quarterly budget report, expected at the next meeting (April 15)
Contract negotiations, set to begin the following week with experienced and new members paired up
